implementation_notes: Scala's actor libraries ship the pattern literally: akka.actor.PoisonPill (and Pekko's equivalent) is a message all actors understand; when the actor processes it, the actor terminates permanently, and because mailboxes are FIFO everything already enqueued ahead of it is handled first. The pill is sent like any other message, so the sender only needs an ActorRef, and one pill per worker stops exactly that worker - no payload type of your own and no queue bookkeeping. Outside actors, Scala uses the JVM primitives: java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue with a poison object, or an ExecutorService whose shutdown() drains queued tasks.
pitfalls: PoisonPill is auto-received: do not add a case PoisonPill in receive - the actor stops when the message is processed, whereas context.stop is immediate and does not drain the mailbox.
Sending PoisonPill to a router or an ActorSelection can stop more actors than intended; address workers individually.
There is no completion acknowledgement - use DeathWatch (context.watch / Terminated) to know the actor actually stopped.
Kill throws ActorKilledException and escalates to supervision; it is not a graceful stop.
